meta.title: NZ Politics 2026: What they actually said

facts: Saturday 7 November 2026. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announced the date on 21 January 2026.

Began on Monday 26 October 2026 (Labour Day), with party leaders among those voting on day one (RNZ, 26 Oct), and runs to Friday 6 November. Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne expects relatively small numbers in the first few days, picking up around the weekend and ramping up on the Thursday and Friday before election day (RNZ live blog, 26 Oct). First figures: Electoral Commission data showed 68,944 people voted on the first day (1.83% of enrolled voters), slightly more than the 65,845 on the first day in 2023; in 2020, when voting opened two days earlier, 105,489 voted on the same day (The Post; Newsroom, 27 Oct). The Commission will not track how many people are turned away because they are not enrolled (Newsroom). Running total: by the end of Tuesday 27 October 175,748 people had voted (4.7% of enrolled voters), including 106,714 on the Tuesday, compared with 146,744 at the same point in 2023 and 366,182 in 2020 (The Post's election dashboard, using daily Electoral Commission figures; it gives the day-one total as 69,034). We could not check the Commission's own site, which blocks our requests. Former Speaker Trevor Mallard (Labour) complained on X that the Wainuiomata advance voting place was closed on day one; Luxon called his comments 'intemperate' (same source). Voting is in person (online voting only for overseas voters). 207 voting places will open on Labour Day (Monday 26 October), offering 1,437 hours of voting, and more will open closer to election day; hours vary, so check vote.nz first. On election day, Saturday 7 November, more than 2,300 voting places will be open from 9am to 7pm. EasyVote cards are not required (Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne, 22 October). Electoral Commission advice released on 18 October called the date 'challenging, but manageable', partly because voting opens on a public holiday.

Closed at midnight on Sunday 25 October 2026 (RNZ, 26 October). You cannot enrol or update details after that, and you cannot enrol at a voting place. Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said every complete application received by the deadline will be processed in time, including forms arriving in the post on Tuesday 27 October; enrolment events were held around the country on the final weekend (RNZ, 23 October). On 25 October Le Quesne told TVNZ's Q+A it was 'fair' to say the earlier deadline would affect the number enrolled, but 'hard to say' how much; the Commission will analyse the impact after the election (RNZ, 1News). Labour said some people had struck problems with the online enrolment form; the Commission said it was not aware of any technical issues (RNZ live blog, 25 Oct).

The final enrolment figure, due on Thursday 29 October, had not been published when we checked at about 8:20am that day; The Post's dashboard gives 92.80% (3,759,992 of an estimated 4,051,640 eligible, about 291,600 not enrolled) as at 26 October. Latest (provisional): on 27 October the Electoral Commission's figures put enrolment at 92.8% of eligible people and 71.2% of 18–24-year-olds, with forms still being processed and the final count due this week; Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said matching 2023's 94.7% would be 'a bit of a stretch' (RNZ live blog, 27 Oct; The Post, which gives 3,759,992 enrolled). Newsroom reported provisional data putting the unenrolled at nearly 300,000. Luxon told Morning Report on 27 October he expected enrolment to end up around or above 2014 (92.6%) and 2017 (92.4%) levels; Labour's Tangi Utikere called the coalition's changes 'anti-democratic' (RNZ). Earlier: on 26 October the Electoral Commission said about 92.5% of eligible voters were enrolled after a weekend flood of enrolments, with the final figure still being counted and expected on Thursday 29 October (RNZ live blog, 26 Oct; RNZ on 27 Oct described the 92.5% as the position as of Friday). Before that: as of Friday 23 October, with two days left, 92.4% of eligible people had enrolled, compared with 94.7% in 2023 (RNZ, 26 Oct), and about 70% of 18–24-year-olds, compared with about 77% on election day 2023 (1News, 25 Oct). These broadly match the unverified figures below. Final enrolment figures had not been published when we checked. Earlier: as at 21 October, 3,729,667 people were enrolled, 92.1% of eligible voters, below the 94.7% reached in 2023 but already more than the 3,688,292 enrolled at that election. 18–24-year-olds remain the least enrolled (302,475, or 68.6%). These are Electoral Commission figures released on 22 October (RNZ). (An earlier RNZ report on 22 October gave 91.2% and 65.5%; the Commission's newer release supersedes it.) A later Commission release, reported only by a secondary source we could read (The Gist, 24 Oct; the Commission's own site blocks our checks), gave 92.2% enrolled and 307,991 eligible people still unenrolled as at 23 October, with 18–24-year-olds on 69.9% (77.2% in 2023); treat these as unverified. Enrol online at vote.nz, by post or at an enrolment hub. Same-day enrolment during advance voting and on election day has been abolished.

Opened on Wednesday 21 October 2026, along with telephone dictation voting for blind and some disabled voters. About 126,000 enrolled voters have told the Electoral Commission they live overseas (92,600 in 2023), 64% of them in Australia (Electoral Commission figures, RNZ live blog, 21 October). By 25 October Le Quesne said more than 132,000 New Zealanders overseas had enrolled, about two-thirds of them in Australia, and just over 20,000 had downloaded voting papers; the Commission sent 2.2 million email reminders, followed by texts (RNZ, 25 Oct). Some overseas voters reported that Adobe Reader's 'Fill & Sign' tool would not let them tick some parties' circles; the Commission said the voting paper is a standard PDF, not a fillable form, that voters can annotate manually, use another reader or print and fill it in by hand, and that a vote counts as long as the voter's intention is clear (1News, 24 Oct).

Coming up: the Q+A People's Debate, with audience questions to figures from National, Labour, the Greens, ACT, NZ First, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity, is live on TVNZ1, TVNZ+ and RNZ at 7pm on Thursday 5 November (1News, 28 Oct). Whakaata Māori's Whakatau 2026 Māori leaders' debate, moderated by Moana Maniapoto, was held on Wednesday 28 October with Tama Potaka (National), Marama Davidson (Greens), Willie Jackson (Labour), Debbie Ngarewa-Packer (Te Pāti Māori) and Shane Jones (NZ First) (Te Ao Māori News). Local: a Waitaki candidates' forum in Wānaka on 27 October included ACT leader David Seymour (RNZ). Earlier: the third and final Luxon v Hipkins head-to-head (Stuff and The Post) was held on Tuesday 20 October. The NZ Herald 'Powerbrokers' debate, moderated by Ryan Bridge, was held on Wednesday 21 October with Marama Davidson (Greens), David Seymour (ACT), Winston Peters (NZ First) and Qiulae Wong (Opportunity). Te Pāti Māori did not take part after the death of co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer's mother (RNZ live blog, 21 October).

The official count is due on Friday 27 November 2026. Luxon said formal coalition talks would probably wait for it, and neither he nor Hipkins would promise a deal before Christmas (RNZ, 19 October). On 26 October Hipkins changed tack and committed to forming a Labour-led government before Christmas (RNZ); Luxon said 'it'll take as long as it takes' (RNZ live blog).
The 54th Parliament was dissolved on 1 October 2026. Ministers stay in office until a new government is formed.
This will not be held with the 2026 election. The government dropped the planned referendum on 18 February 2026 (secondary source: Wikipedia).

context: The current government is the Sixth National Government, formed in November 2023. National leads it with two separate coalition agreements, one with ACT and one with NZ First. Winston Peters was Deputy Prime Minister until 31 May 2025, when David Seymour took over under the agreed rotation.
Seats at dissolution: National 49, ACT 11 and NZ First 8 (government total 68). Labour 34, Greens 15, Te Pāti Māori 4 and two independents (both former Te Pāti Māori MPs). That is 123 seats in total.

Polls in the final month show both major parties well below their 2023 results (64.9% together), and the two latest polls, taken over almost the same days, disagree on who leads. The RNZ–Reid Research poll (20–26 October, 1000 eligible voters online, ±3.1%, published 29 October) had Labour on 30.6% (down 0.2) and National on 24.8% (down 1.1), below its 2020 result of 25.6%; Greens 14.5%, ACT 10.1% (up 1.1, ahead of NZ First), NZ First 9.9%, Opportunity 7.2% (up 1.7) and Te Pāti Māori 1.9%. On RNZ's projection Labour (37 seats), the Greens (18) and Opportunity (9) would have 64 of 120 seats and the coalition 54, assuming Te Pāti Māori wins one or two electorates. Preferred PM: Hipkins 23.3% (up 1.4), Luxon 17.1%; 53.8% said Luxon was doing poorly as PM and 30.1% well, while Hipkins' rating turned positive (39.7% well, 34.7% poorly). 50.5% said the country was heading in the wrong direction (RNZ, 29 Oct). National campaign chair Simeon Brown said the poll was 'out of step with most of the other polls that we're seeing, including our own'; Seymour called some movements an 'outlier'; Hipkins said it showed 'real momentum' for change. The 1News–Verian poll (21–25 October, 1000 eligible voters, ±3.1%, published 27 October) had National down three points to 29% (28.9%) and Labour unchanged on 27% (27.3%), Labour's fifth poll in a row in the upper 20s; Greens 15% (14.8%), ACT 12% (12.4%, a term high), NZ First 10%, Opportunity 6% (6.3%) and Te Pāti Māori 0.1%, its lowest in the series (it is running a candidate-vote-only campaign). On 1News' projections National, ACT and NZ First would have 61 seats: enough to govern if Te Pāti Māori wins only one electorate (a 121-seat Parliament), but two short of the 63 needed if it holds four seats and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi keeps Te Tai Tokerau (125 seats), in which case Opportunity's eight MPs would decide. The left bloc (Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori, Kapa-Kingi) would have 56 seats in that scenario and 64 with Opportunity. Preferred PM: Luxon 24% (up four, his best of the campaign), Hipkins 18%. 11% were undecided or refused on the party vote (1News, 27 Oct; RNZ). Luxon said 'the only poll that matters is November 7th'; Hipkins said it would come down to turnout; Peters said 'we don't believe in these polls'. A week earlier (15–19 October) the same poll had National 32% and Labour 27%, while The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll (9–19 October, published 20 October) had Labour narrowly ahead (28.7% v 27.6%) with Opportunity on 5.4%. Earlier, the 13 October Verian poll had the majors tied on 28%, and a leaked 6–10 October Anacta poll (Labour's own pollster) had Labour 29%, National 28%.

Leader ratings: in 1News Vote Compass (136,713 participants, 4–11 October, weighted, non-probability), no leader averaged 5 out of 10 for favourability. Hipkins was highest on 4.3, then Swarbrick 4.0, Wong 3.8, Peters 3.7 and Luxon 3.6; Seymour 3.4, Davidson 3.3, Ngarewa-Packer 2.1 and Waititi 1.9 (1News, 17 Oct).

Health: in the 20 October 1News–Verian poll 70% of voters said the public health system is in crisis and 28% said it faces challenges but is not in crisis (1News, 20 Oct). Health has become the second-biggest campaign issue after the cost of living, and dominated the final leaders' debate.

Cost of living and schools: in the same 15–19 October 1News–Verian poll (published 21 October), National and Labour were tied on 28% as the party voters most trust to tackle the cost of living, ahead of the Greens (10%), ACT (7%), NZ First (6%), Opportunity (3%) and Te Pāti Māori (1%); 17% named none or did not know. 70% wanted to keep the rule that primary schools teach an hour each of reading, writing and maths every day, and 24% wanted it removed (1News, 21 Oct).

Inflation: annual inflation eased to 3.7% in the September quarter, from 4.1% (Stats NZ, 22 October), and is expected to rise again once the fuel-price spike is captured. Nicola Willis called it encouraging; Labour's Willow-Jean Prime pointed to unemployment at an 11-year high and 30,000 more people on Jobseeker; David Seymour said that without fuel prices inflation was within the Reserve Bank's band (RNZ; RNZ live blog, 22 Oct). On 28 October the Reserve Bank unexpectedly held the official cash rate at 2.75% in a split decision, when a rise had been expected (1News). Willis said a Labour-led 'four-headed' coalition would put lower rates at risk; Labour's Barbara Edmonds said Willis was 'celebrating a sluggish economy'; Swarbrick said 'higher mortgage prices cannot reopen the Strait of Hormuz' (RNZ live blog, 28 Oct).

Late deciders: in the final Post/Freshwater Strategy poll (9–19 October, 1458 voters, ±3%), only 14% said they always vote for the same party; 34% had decided in the past few months (12% in the past few weeks) and 15% were still undecided. Half planned to vote on election day and 34% during advance voting. 26% of NZ First supporters and 23% of Opportunity supporters had decided in the past few weeks. In Auckland (426 likely voters) National led Labour 37.7% to 26.4%, while Hipkins was preferred PM over Luxon 45.9% to 41.1% (The Post, 23 Oct; The Post, 22 Oct).

Tax on the wealthy: in 1News Vote Compass (186,475 participants, 4–21 October, weighted, non-probability), 62% said wealthier people should pay somewhat or much more tax, down from 67% in 2023 but a majority in every Vote Compass survey since 2014, including 53% of those earning over $100,000. By current party support: Greens 96%, Labour 88%, Opportunity 86%, NZ First 45%, National 30%, ACT 25% (1News, 24 Oct).

Where voters differ from their party: 1News Vote Compass (185,371 participants, 4–27 October, weighted, non-probability) found the generational tobacco-sales ban was the biggest gap for all three coalition parties: each strongly opposes it, but their supporters lean towards supporting it (National supporters averaged 3.66 on a 1–5 scale). The biggest gap overall was Te Pāti Māori's opposition to a cap on council rates (its supporters averaged 4.12); for Labour it was transgender women in sport, and for Opportunity limits on rent increases (1News, 29 Oct).

Big issues of 2026: the cost of living (made worse by a fuel-price spike linked to the 2026 Middle East conflict); tax (Labour's capital gains tax, the Greens' wealth taxes, National's 'no new taxes' pledge); two challenges to Luxon's leadership inside National (April and August); the law replacing the RMA, passed in September; Treaty and Waitangi Tribunal policy; immigration; and turmoil inside Te Pāti Māori.
meta.other_parties_note: Te Tai Tokerau Party was founded in May 2026 by Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, the sitting MP for Te Tai Tokerau, after her split from Te Pāti Māori. Its list has two names (Kyla Campbell-Kamariera and Kapa-Kingi). It is not profiled in depth here. It is listed because 1News counts it in the left bloc's seat projections if Kapa-Kingi holds her seat.

parties.name: New Zealand National Party
parties.selection: The leader plus list places 2 to 5 on National's 2026 list (released 8 August 2026): deputy leader Nicola Willis (2), Chris Bishop (3), Simeon Brown (4) and Erica Stanford (5). All four are senior Cabinet ministers.
parties.history: Founded in 1936 from a merger of the United and Reform parties. It is New Zealand's main centre-right party and has led governments under Holland, Holyoake, Muldoon, Bolger/Shipley and Key/English. It won the most votes in 2023 and formed the current government with ACT and NZ First.
parties.ideology: Centre-right. Liberal-conservative, pro-market, and focused on fiscal restraint, law and order, and 'getting the basics right'.
parties.role: Leads the Sixth National Government (since 27 November 2023) under separate coalition agreements with ACT and NZ First. Christopher Luxon is Prime Minister and Nicola Willis is Minister of Finance.
policies: 100-day plan (25 October 2026, Luxon at a rally in Browns Bay, Auckland): 26 actions, mostly compiled from earlier campaign announcements. They include introducing KiwiSaver changes, a trade mission to India, passing the rates cap (2–4%), legislation to extend paid parental leave to 27 weeks from July 2027 (on the way to 30), Commerce Commission powers and a report on separating Foodstuffs within six months, lifting the First Home Loan income cap to $300,000, cutting student loan repayments from 12 to 10 cents in the dollar, free cervical screening for women aged 25 to 69, a bill banning taxpayer funding of gangs, active-consent laws and an Auckland Transport Police team. Hipkins called it 'rehashing announcement after reannouncement'; Seymour said 'some things that will go ahead, others that won't'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2141781/national-sets-out-first-actions-if-re-elected-in-100-day-plan

Plan for parents (24 October 2026, Luxon in Auckland): financial literacy added to the school curriculum from Year 1 to Year 10 (Erica Stanford: saving, spending and giving, being sensible with money), and changes to anti-money-laundering rules to make it easier to open a bank account for a child. The rest restates earlier commitments (three-day postnatal stays, the $1500 KiwiSaver 'Baby Boost', the solar home energy fund, 30 weeks' paid parental leave); Luxon said there was 'a lot of packaging up of things that we have announced already'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2122803/as-it-happened-election-campaign-24-october

Plan for young adults (23 October 2026, Luxon): a package restating earlier commitments: lower student loan repayment rates for borrowers living in New Zealand, wider access to 5% first-home deposits, paid parental leave extended from 26 to 30 weeks, compulsory KiwiSaver with higher contributions and a $1500 'Baby Boost' for newborns, more intensive employment support for long-term jobseekers, and no new taxes.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261023-young-adults

Housing for older people (22 October 2026, Luxon in Papamoa): at least 20% of Housing Flexible Fund places reserved for people aged 65 and over, with no extra funding; granny-flat consent exemptions extended to tiny homes on wheels and to empty sections; and the repeated promise that employers keep paying KiwiSaver for over-65s still contributing. The Christchurch Methodist Mission welcomed the ring-fencing but called for a bigger fund so families are not squeezed out.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2074549/national-promises-more-affordable-homes-for-older-people

Plan for Kiwi Kids (21 October 2026, Luxon and Erica Stanford in Pongakawa): mostly existing policies (KiwiSaver BabyBoost, screens out of ECE, the school phone ban, replacing NCEA, keeping students at school to the end of Year 11). The one new policy expands the Maths Acceleration Programme so 40,000 more Year 7–10 students can take part over three years (75,900 are already funded for 2027–29); students must be at least a year behind the curriculum.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2051719/national-promises-to-expand-maths-acceleration-programme
'No new taxes': on 23 August 2026 Luxon widened the pledge from 'no new taxes on working people' and ruled out a bank tax and a bed (accommodation) tax.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1083119/national-promises-no-new-taxes-if-re-elected
Welfare: Jobseeker changes announced 8 October 2026, including random drug testing ('If you can work, you should').
https://x.com/chrisluxonmp/status/2107949741086765497
Education: NCEA to be replaced by new qualifications (NZCE at Year 12, NZACE at Year 13). Details were confirmed in May 2026.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/595424/government-confirms-ncea-replacement-details
Planning: the Planning Act and Natural Environment Act replacing the RMA passed on 22 September 2026. The full system is intended to be running by 2030.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/260922-chrisbishop
Social media: a bill to ban under-16s from most social media platforms was introduced as a National Party bill in August 2026. ACT and NZ First oppose it (secondary source).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand

Fiscal plan (12 October 2026): tax relief only once the books are back in surplus (not forecast before 2029); a commitment to an independent election policy-costing unit by the 2029 election; $451.8m to extend the school lunch programme to the next election.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1858565/national-hints-at-tax-cuts-after-2029-as-fiscal-plan-released

Superannuation: National confirmed its fiscal plan is its super policy. It still proposes raising the age gradually but sets no date, and commits to cross-party talks within 100 days of a new government.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1860419/politicians-can-t-dance-alone-on-superannuation-nicola-willis
Aid: a plan to cut aid outside the Pacific to fund health spending. Coalition partner NZ First publicly criticised it.
https://x.com/winstonpeters/status/2107229536366850450

Young New Zealanders (13 October 2026): five commitments to legislate or direct in the first 100 days: lower student loan repayment rates for borrowers living in New Zealand, wider access to 5% deposits for first-home buyers, paid parental leave extended from 26 to 30 weeks within three years, a $1500 KiwiSaver 'Baby Boost', and faster visas for partners of New Zealand citizens. National says each is funded to start by 1 July 2027.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/261013-nicolawillis

Plug-in solar (15 October 2026): shops able to sell plug-in solar panels within six months of a re-elected National government, once safety rules being developed with Australia are finished; a Home Energy Fund for rooftop solar, batteries, insulation and heat pumps, repaid through rates; and rooftop solar without a consent.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/261015-simeonbrown-1

Auckland plan (14 October 2026): remove the blanket ban on minimum car-parking requirements and let councils set minimums in suburban areas outside intensification zones, greenfield subdivisions and business parks. Most of the nine-page plan restates enacted or already announced policies.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1887747/national-promises-to-remove-auckland-s-ban-on-minimum-car-parking-rules

Right to silence (18 October 2026, Paul Goldsmith): a new Crimes Act offence of not giving police information when a child under 12 is killed and it is clear one or more adults were present at or before the death, with a maximum of 10 years' prison. National says it would work with legal experts on a narrow exception to the right to silence. Child Matters said the idea needs careful scrutiny.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1978144/national-pledges-to-take-away-right-to-silence-when-a-child-is-murdered

Waikato (19 October 2026, Chris Bishop): if re-elected, start construction of the SH1 Cambridge to Piarere extension of the Waikato Expressway early next year. Most of the release restates projects already under way or announced (Hamilton Southern Links, the Waikato medical school, fast-track approvals for Green Steel and Waihi North).
https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261019-chrisbishop

Social media (19 October 2026): after Labour's announcement, Luxon matched its promise to progress an under-16 social media ban within a new government's first 100 days, saying it had always been his plan to prioritise it next term.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2010803/as-it-happened-election-campaign-19-october

Agriculture manifesto (16 October 2026, AgFest in Greymouth): 19 sets of nationwide rules (national standards) so farmers can do work such as growing vegetables, storing water, managing animal waste, building farm tracks and housing seasonal workers without council consent if they meet the conditions. No timeline was given, and five of the 19 standards repeat earlier announcements. Also up to 70 graduate vets a year supported to work rurally from 2027 (up to $3.4m over four years) and $16m over four years for wild deer, goat and pest control from the international visitor levy.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1952424/national-promises-fewer-council-approvals-for-farms
events: 28 October 2026: Luxon toured Whanganui, Waverley, Hāwera and New Plymouth with Erica Stanford and Nicola Willis, telling supporters 'we don't need anything funky there, voting tactically' (RNZ live blog). Campaign chair Simeon Brown demanded Labour and the Greens say which smaller-party policies they would accept, but would not say which NZ First promises National would; he said Willis 'will be our finance minister'. Stanford called Opportunity 'a bunch of flakes' on Duncan Garner's podcast and Willis agreed ('a party of flakes'). Willis said the Reserve Bank's OCR hold showed lower rates were at risk under Labour. The RNZ–Reid Research poll published the next morning had National on 24.8%; RNZ's analysis said Willis, Bishop, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee could be at risk on the list, and Goldsmith has written to Epsom voters asking for their electorate vote.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2211552/national-party-mps-feeling-the-pressure-of-party-vote-plunge

28 October 2026: at a Lower Hutt public meeting of more than 450 people, Winston Peters told NZ First supporters to give their electorate vote to National's Chris Bishop in Hutt South, calling him 'a cut above' the usual National MP, while saying it was not an endorsement of National. NZ First's Hutt South candidate Alistair Boyce (35th on its list) backed the move; Bishop said he welcomed support from everyone.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2211837/winston-peters-endorses-national-s-chris-bishop-over-nz-first-s-hutt-south-candidate

27 October 2026: Luxon told Morning Report he expected 2026 enrolment to be 'around or higher' than 2014 and 2017. In Christchurch he and Willis challenged the Greens to name their bottom lines and Labour to say which Green policies it would adopt; he said NZ First candidate Ron Mark was perhaps 'trying to cosplay Pete Hegseth' over his Manawanui ad, but did not rule him out as defence minister. He opened Hamilton Jet's expansion and held an evening rally of about 200 people. After the 1News–Verian poll (National down three to 29%) he said 'the only poll that matters is November 7th'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2174738/election-campaign-27-october-as-it-happened-early-voting-open-with-less-than-two-weeks-to-election-day

28 October 2026 (published): in an interview with RNZ's The Detail, Luxon called Labour's economic record 'financial vandalism on a mass scale', rejected claims his coalition partners had created division, said he would stay for a full term if re-elected, and again ruled out working with Opportunity.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2197471/literally-illiterate-luxon-lashes-labour-s-economic-record

26 October 2026: Luxon voted in Beachlands with his wife Amanda (for Paul Goldsmith and National, he said), then campaigned in Botany. He said the result could come down to 'one or two points', would not promise a government by Christmas, and said he would be comfortable if enrolment ended up lower than in 2023 because 'people have had plenty of time'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2160626/as-it-happened-election-campaign-26-october

25 October 2026: after Mongrel Mob life member Harry Tam posted a photo of Luxon with Black Power members, taken at the Crown apology to abuse-in-care survivors, Luxon said it was different from candidates 'campaigning for their vote' with gangs, and said abuse in state care 'might well play a role' in people joining gangs. Asked about help to leave gangs, he could not name a specific programme. Mark Mitchell said it was 'perverse' for politicians to visit gang pads.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2144805/national-leader-christopher-luxon-warns-not-all-gang-photos-are-the-same

25 October 2026: National removed a Palmerston North campaign volunteer and electorate committee member after learning (following NZ Herald inquiries) that he was convicted in 2021 of sexual conduct with a minor. Luxon said he had only just become aware and 'good on them for doing the right thing'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2153463/national-removes-volunteer-after-learning-of-sexual-conduct-with-minor-conviction

25 October 2026: Luxon rejected claims the earlier enrolment deadline disenfranchised voters ('absolutely not'), after the Chief Electoral Officer said it was 'fair' to say it would affect enrolment numbers. He later campaigned in Taupō with Louise Upston, followed around the Kinloch market by Labour candidate Chris Flatt.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2147586/national-leader-christopher-luxon-labour-s-chris-hipkins-urge-voters-to-enrol

24 October 2026: a photo circulated of National MP and Māori Development Minister Tama Potaka with patched Mongrel Mob members. Potaka told RNZ it was taken at a public Kīngitanga hui in January 2024 when a schoolmate asked for a photo, before the gang patch ban. Luxon said Potaka was 'not campaigning, he's not fundraising' and that it would be 'disingenuous' to equate it with the images of Labour, Green and Te Pāti Māori candidates; Police Minister Mark Mitchell said there was 'a huge difference' between a public event and campaigning at a gang fundraiser.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2124931/luxon-defends-potaka-on-photo-with-gang-members

24 October 2026, Auckland waterfront walkabout with Auckland Central candidate Candace Kinser: Luxon said he did not know what Crate Day was when a stag party suggested it become a national holiday (RNZ live blog).

parties.name: New Zealand Labour Party
parties.selection: The leader plus list places 2 to 5 on Labour's list (released 8 June 2026): deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni, finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds, Willie Jackson and Megan Woods.
parties.history: Founded in 1916 and New Zealand's oldest current party. It built the welfare state under Savage (1935) and has led governments under Fraser, Nash, Kirk, Lange, Clark and Ardern/Hipkins. It lost power in 2023 after two terms.
parties.role: Official Opposition. Chris Hipkins (Prime Minister January to November 2023) is leader and is seeking to form a government with the Greens and, potentially, Te Pāti Māori and/or Opportunity.

parties.history: Founded in 1993–94 by Roger Douglas and Derek Quigley, architects of 1980s economic reform. It has held Epsom since 2008. It grew from one MP to ten in 2020 and won 11 seats (8.64%) in 2023.
parties.ideology: Right. Classical liberal and libertarian-leaning: smaller government, lower taxes, deregulation, and 'equal rights' (opposing race-based policy).
parties.role: Coalition partner in government. David Seymour has been Deputy Prime Minister since 31 May 2025 and is Minister for Regulation. The Regulatory Standards Act passed in November 2025.

It drops ACT's September pledge to scrap the Permanent Resident Visa: existing PR holders are unaffected, but future holders would have to live in New Zealand at least two years in every five to keep it. It also includes the KiwiSaver earnings tax cut, raising the super age to 67 by 2035, electronic payment management for work-ready Jobseekers after four months, a three-year adult minimum wage freeze with a 60% training wage for under-20s, $400m more for GPs, a national cancer centre, and scrapping the Climate Change Commission and Zero Carbon Act.

parties.name: New Zealand First
parties.selection: The leader plus list places 2 to 5 (list released 7 October 2026): deputy leader Shane Jones, Casey Costello, Mark Patterson and Alfred Ngaro (a former National minister, not a current MP).
parties.history: Founded by Winston Peters in 1993 after he left National. It has been in government with National (1996–98, 2023–) and Labour (2005–08 confidence and supply; 2017–20 coalition). It was out of Parliament in 2008–11 and 2020–23, and returned in 2023 with 8 seats.
parties.ideology: Nationalist and populist. Socially conservative and economically interventionist in places ('common sense'). Opposes what it calls race-based policy and 'woke' policy.
parties.role: Coalition partner in government. Peters is Minister of Foreign Affairs (and was Deputy PM until May 2025). Shane Jones holds Resources, Regional Development and Oceans and Fisheries.
policies: 'Commonsense Express' 10-point rail plan (27 October 2026, Peters at a public meeting in Levin): nearly $4b in total, much of it already allocated or underway, including the Rail Network Investment Programme, the Marsden Point Rail Link, new Cook Strait ferries in 2029, making Te Huia permanent ($130m for new trains), permanent Christchurch passenger rail, level-crossing removals ($300m), Kaimai Tunnel capacity, Auckland and Wellington rail companies co-owned by taxpayers and ratepayers, and planning for Auckland's third and fourth main lines.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2193460/nz-first-announces-4b-commonsense-express-plan-for-rail

Fuel and the ETS (24 October 2026, Peters at a public meeting in Thames): remove the Emissions Trading Scheme charge from fuel over the next term, which NZ First says would cut about 12 cents a litre off petrol and 14 cents off diesel; it says the ETS took $850m from fuel consumers and businesses in the past year.

Accelerated depreciation (23 October 2026, Peters at Pact Packaging, East Tāmaki): a 50% first-year depreciation rate for new plant, machinery and equipment in manufacturing and targeted export sectors (mining, aquaculture, forestry, farming, fishing), on top of the existing 20% Investment Boost, to be implemented at the next Budget. Peters put the cost at $2.4b in 2026/27 and $2.5b in 2027/28.

Law and order (22 October 2026, Peters in West Auckland): a degrees-of-murder regime raising the minimum non-parole period from 10 to 20 years, life without parole for first-degree murder and for the rape or murder of children, an eight-year minimum non-parole period for fatal 'coward punches', investigating 'stand your ground' self-defence laws, and replacing the Serious Fraud Office with a Police division plus a dedicated organised crime agency.

parties.selection: Both co-leaders plus the party's other two sitting MPs (Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke and Oriini Kaipara), party president John Tamihere, and general secretary Lance Norman, who is the only name on TPM's 2026 party list. Tamihere and Norman are not MPs.
parties.history: Founded in 2004 (as the Māori Party) after the foreshore and seabed controversy. It supported National-led governments in 2008–17, was out of Parliament in 2017–20, and returned in 2020. In 2023 it won 6 of the 7 Māori electorates.
parties.ideology: Kaupapa Māori. Tino rangatiratanga, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and generally left-leaning on economic policy.
parties.role: Opposition. It is running a candidate-vote-only strategy: it asks Māori-roll voters for their electorate vote in all seven Māori seats, aims to create an overhang, and submitted a one-person party list.
policies: Candidate-vote ('one tick') strategy across the seven Māori electorates, with a one-person list.

parties.name: The Opportunity Party (formerly TOP)
parties.status: Not in Parliament. Polling around or above 5%
parties.selection: Leader Qiulae Wong and deputy leader Daniel Eb (list places 1 and 2). As a party outside Parliament it gets a shorter profile.
parties.history: Founded in 2016 by economist Gareth Morgan as The Opportunities Party (TOP). It has never won a seat (2.22% in 2023). Qiulae Wong became leader in November 2025 and the party rebranded as The Opportunity Party.
parties.ideology: Self-described centrist, 'evidence-based' and radical centrist. Wong says supporters are 'politically homeless'. A Talbot Mills analysis found about a third of its supporters came from the left and a third from the right (secondary source).
parties.role: Outside Parliament. The 29 October RNZ–Reid Research poll put it on 7.2% (nine seats), enough to give Labour and the Greens a majority; the 27 October 1News–Verian poll had it on 6% (6.3%, eight seats; 7% a week earlier), enough to decide the result unless Te Pāti Māori wins only one electorate; the final Post/Freshwater Strategy poll (20 October) had it on 5.4%, just over the threshold. Luxon has again ruled out working with it; ACT's David Seymour said on 15 October he would be open to a bloc including it. Wong says Opportunity will speak first to the largest party by seats on election night, and won't support a government with Winston Peters as foreign minister.
policies: Future Generations Commissioner (25 October 2026, Wong on TVNZ's Q+A): a Future Generations Act creating an independent officer of Parliament with a five-year term to guide long-term national goals and run citizens' assemblies; major policies, Budgets and investment proposals would have to disclose long-term costs and impacts, including the cost of 'doing nothing'. Wong put the cost at about $5m a year. It would have no power to force governments to act. Luxon called it 'more waffle' (without having seen it); Hipkins was open to talking but sceptical.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2141298/opportunity-to-set-up-future-generations-commissioner-for-government-s-long-term-impacts

Five post-election bottom lines: a stronger Commerce Commission; lobbying regulation and donation caps; a 10-year health plan; phasing out bottom trawling; and recommitting to the Paris Agreement with an independent Climate Change Commission.

people.name: Christopher Luxon
people.role: Prime Minister; Leader of the National Party; Minister for National Security and Intelligence
people.seat: MP for Botany (since 2020); contesting Botany
people.background: Former chief executive of Air New Zealand and a former Unilever executive. Entered Parliament in 2020, became National leader in November 2021 and Prime Minister in November 2023.
positions: 'No new taxes' (no bank tax, no bed tax); tough welfare obligations, including drug testing for Jobseekers.
Has ruled out working with the Opportunity Party because of its land value tax; calls vote-splitting 'insanely stupid'.
Campaigns on economic 'turnaround' and 'fixing the basics'.
reversals: National's tax pledge was originally 'no new taxes on working people'. In August 2026 Luxon widened it to 'no new taxes', dropping a bank tax and bed tax that ministers (including Willis) had floated earlier in the year.

In early May 2026 Luxon said National would 'go to the election with another election policy around superannuation and lifting the retirement age for sure'. Its 12 October fiscal plan set no date for raising the age and committed to cross-party talks instead. National says its stance has not changed.

quotes.text: We're just better managers of money. They sucked. They were literally illiterate.
quotes.context: On Labour's economic record, in an interview with RNZ's The Detail (published 28 Oct).

quotes.text: When the world throws a shock at you, that's exactly when you want a steady government that's careful with your money.
quotes.context: Browns Bay rally speech, referring to high fuel prices (RNZ live blog).

quotes.text: It's a crime issue, law and order issue, not a race issue.
quotes.context: Rejecting Hipkins' claim that racism was a factor in the Leoni affair (RNZ live blog).

quotes.text: Yes, that instinctively is a position of the National Party. But I do want to work in a cross-party way with Chris to try and have a proper conversation about retirement.
quotes.context: Final Stuff leaders' debate, on raising the superannuation age.

quotes.text: no, we're going to win, it's very simple.
quotes.context: Asked whether ruling out Opportunity meant he would rather be in opposition than in a coalition with it (RNZ live blog).

quotes.text: They were in the room where it happened, as Hamilton would say, and I'm not quite sure what they're banging on about today, because that is not quite right.
quotes.context: Responding to coalition partner NZ First's fast-track housing policy, which he called 'quite bizarre' because it was already law.

quotes.text: He can't find a pathway to get into government without those four radical parties and six leaders, that's going to be chaos.
quotes.context: On Chris Hipkins' likely coalition partners (Greens, Te Pāti Māori, Opportunity), RNZ Morning Report.

quotes.text: We've been doing a big turnaround, we've been fixing a lot of the basics. We now have an opportunity, as this recovery comes through, not just to watch it come through but to actually shape the future of this country...
quotes.context: Election-date announcement; pitching National's economic record.

people.name: Nicola Willis
people.role: Deputy Leader of the National Party; Minister of Finance; Minister for Economic Growth; Minister for Social Investment
people.seat: List MP; list rank 2 (not contesting an electorate)
people.background: Entered Parliament on the list in 2018 after a career as a political adviser and corporate lobbyist. Deputy leader since December 2021; Finance Minister since 2023; delivered Budget 2026 on 28 May.
positions: Fiscal restraint in an election year. Calls Labour's fiscal plan 'the least credible… in living memory'.
Personally favours raising the NZ Super age gradually. National's 2026 policy is cross-party talks within 100 days rather than a set date.

Tax relief only once the books are back in surplus (not forecast before 2029). On 14 October she signalled interest in future business tax relief (including the R&D tax credit and, over time, the corporate rate) alongside personal tax cuts when conditions allow.
Floated taxing banks 'fairly' in May 2026, then dropped it under the 'no new taxes' pledge.
reversals: In May 2026 she said 'We've got to make sure the banks are taxed fairly…'. On 23 August 2026 she explained why National would not pursue a bank tax.

quotes.text: So ask yourself: if interest rates are rising now, even with the government spending responsibly, how much higher would they go under a Labour coalition that increases government spending?
quotes.context: Responding to the Reserve Bank holding the OCR at 2.75% (RNZ live blog).

quotes.text: We have been fixing the underlying foundations, and New Zealand will be seeing the rewards if we stick to the plan.
quotes.context: Media stand-up on the September-quarter inflation figures (RNZ live blog).

quotes.text: I'm really interested in the R&D tax credit, which has been successful in encouraging firms to invest in innovation, and there's potential for expanding that. And I think over time, looking at that top-line corporate rate, yes, we're not as competitive as we would like to be with the rest of the developed world.
quotes.context: Same RNZ interview on corporate tax and R&D credits.

quotes.text: While our fiscal plan shows a pathway to potential tax relief for working New Zealanders, now is not the time to cut taxes.
quotes.context: Releasing National's fiscal plan with Christopher Luxon

quotes.text: I have looked at what the banks are being taxed at now and measures for changing that, and there are no other measures that I can see won't result in additional costs for Kiwis.
quotes.context: Explaining why National dropped a bank tax under its 'no new taxes' pledge.

quotes.text: I will go to the campaign trail as the National Party finance spokesperson with my view on what would be appropriate, well signalled, fair, transparent, gradual, gradual changes to New Zealand superannuation.

quotes.text: Kiwis can look forward with confidence, they just need to choose it, they just need to vote for it.
quotes.context: Closing line of her Budget 2026 speech.

quotes.text: One for all, all for one. And when the caucus, by majority, have confidence in the leader, then we all stand together, backing the leader.
quotes.context: As deputy leader, after Luxon survived the April caucus confidence vote.

people.name: Chris Bishop
people.role: Attorney-General (since April 2026); Minister of Housing; Infrastructure; Transport; RMA Reform
people.seat: MP for Hutt South; contesting Hutt South
people.background: First entered Parliament as a list MP in 2014. Leader of the House until April 2026, and campaign chair until the April reshuffle, when he became Attorney-General. Led the RMA replacement and the first National Infrastructure Plan.
positions: Planning reform: says the new system should make fast-track unnecessary within five years.
Backed Luxon in the April confidence vote, describing the caucus discussion as 'good, honest and robust'.

quotes.text: I'll be working hard for as many votes as possible everyday until November 7.
quotes.context: Responding to Winston Peters' endorsement of him in Hutt South.

quotes.text: If re-elected, National will get it under construction early next year.
quotes.context: National release 'Backing Waikato', on the SH1 Cambridge to Piarere extension of the Waikato Expressway.

quotes.text: The blanket ban on minimum car parking requirements has not worked. The economic theory behind it did not account for the reality of New Zealand's suburban streets.
quotes.context: Launching National's Auckland plan as transport spokesperson.

quotes.text: They've literally released a press release that says they will change the law to do things that are already in the law.
quotes.context: On coalition partner NZ First's fast-track housing policy.

quotes.text: Today is a major milestone. After 35 years of the RMA, Parliament has passed legislation for a fundamentally different way of planning for New Zealand's future.
quotes.context: Press release as the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill (RMA replacement) passed third reading.

quotes.text: Passing these Bills is not the end of the job. The next task is making sure the new system works in practice.
quotes.context: Same release; the full new system is intended to operate by 2030.

quotes.text: I think what the Prime Minister was saying, which I would broadly agree with, is that the country has very difficult challenges ahead of it and we should spend our time focused on those challenges.

quotes.text: Obviously I love being the campaign chair, and it's a role I enjoy doing, but it's fine - I've got plenty of things to do.
quotes.context: After losing the campaign-chair and Leader of the House roles in the April reshuffle while becoming Attorney-General.

people.name: Simeon Brown
people.role: Minister of Health; Minister for Energy; State Owned Enterprises; National campaign chair (since April 2026)
people.seat: MP for Pakuranga (since 2017); contesting Pakuranga

quotes.text: Ultimately, it's out of step with most of the other polls that we're seeing, including our own.

quotes.context: Press conference as National's campaign chair, attacking the Greens' fiscal plan (RNZ live blog).

quotes.text: Another glossy document and another review won't fix a single ED. Labour had six years to get this right, and performance went backwards on its watch.
quotes.context: Responding to Labour's emergency-department plan.

quotes.text: Making your own power should be as easy as plugging in a toaster.
quotes.context: As National's energy spokesperson, announcing that shops would be able to sell plug-in solar panels within six months of a re-elected National government.

quotes.text: I'm focused on making sure that we win in November and making sure that we deliver a National-led government.

quotes.text: These changes are about ensuring treatments are safe and carefully managed, while maintaining access to care for those who need it.

people.name: Erica Stanford
people.role: Minister of Education; Minister of Immigration; lead minister on the Royal Commission (abuse in care) response
people.seat: MP for East Coast Bays (since 2017); contesting East Coast Bays

people.seat: MP for Remutaka (since 2008); contesting Remutaka
